questions.question: Question 1
questions.solution_html:
• Actual Breach
  • • Definition: It occurs when a party fails to perform their contractual obligation on or after the date
  • of performance.
  • • Timing: Happens at the time performance is due.
  • • Cause: The party does not fulfill their promise as stated in the contract.
  • • Example: A supplier who has received payment but fails to deliver goods by the agreed date
  • commits an actual breach.
  • • Remedy: The aggrieved party may demand performance, claim damages, or take legal action for
  • compensation.
  • Indemnity: One party compensates another for a loss.
  • At Promisor’s Desire: The act or abstinence must be done at the promisor’s request, not
  • voluntarily or at a third party’s request.
  • Natural Love and Affection: Written and registered agreement between close relatives.
  • Destruction of Subject Matter
  • If the essential subject matter is destroyed without fault of either party.
  • Example: Taylor v. Caldwell (1863) – music hall destroyed by fire.
  • Suit for Price (Section 55)
  • Meaning
  • A legal action by the seller to recover the full agreed price of the goods from the buyer.
  • When Available
  • • Ownership of the goods has passed to the buyer, but the buyer refuses to pay; or
  • • The contract specifies that payment is due on a fixed date, even if ownership has not
  • passed.
  • Purpose
  • To recover the entire contract price for goods sold or agreed to be sold.
  • Written Instrument: Must be in writing (handwritten, printed, or typed).
  • Open (Bearer) Cheque: Payable to whoever holds and presents it. Transferable by delivery.
  • Order Cheque: Payable to a named person or their order; needs endorsement for transfer.
  • Specific Goods
  • • Definition: Identified and agreed upon at the contract.
  • • Rule: Passes according to parties’ intention.
  • • Default
  • o Deliverable goods → ownership passes when contract is made.
  • o Goods need preparation/price fixing → passes after preparation and buyer notification.
  • Impact on Employee Morale
  • • Perception of Unfairness: Employees feel appraisals are based on gender, race, or favoritism
  • creating a sense of injustice.
  • • Reduced Motivation and Engagement: Unrecognized effort or unequal treatment leads to
  • demotivation and lower productivity.
  • • Increased Stress and Anxiety: Fear of biased reviews affects mental health.
  • • Erosion of Trust: Employees lose confidence in management and the appraisal process.
  • • Higher Turnover: Demoralized employees leave, increasing recruitment and training costs.
  • Ethical Concerns in Privacy and Data Collection in Online Marketing
questions.final_answer: Ethical Concerns in Privacy and Data Collection in Online Marketing

questions.question: Question 2
questions.solution_html:
• Anticipatory Breach
  • • Definition: It occurs when one party clearly indicates, through words or conduct, before the due
  • date, that they will not perform their contractual obligations. It is also called a constructive
  • breach.
  • • Timing: Occurs before the performance date arrives.
  • • Cause: The defaulting party gives advance notice—explicitly or implicitly—of non-performance.
  • • Example: A builder informs the client before the deadline that they are going out of business and
  • cannot complete the project.
  • • Remedy: The non-breaching party can immediately terminate the contract or seek remedies
  • without waiting for the performance date, allowing them to minimize potential losses.
  • Key Difference
  • • Actual breach occurs on or after the date of performance, while anticipatory breach occurs before
  • the date of performance.
  • or
  • 11b. Explain the various types of special contracts in brief.
  • b
  • .A. Types of Contracts
  • . 1. Valid Contract: Legally enforceable agreement with all essential elements.
  • Void Contract: Not enforceable by law; has no legal effect.
  • Guarantee: A third party assures performance or payment if another fails.
  • Legal Value (Not Adequate): Must have legal value but need not be equal; even a
  • nominal item (peppercorn theory) is valid.
  • Past Voluntary Services: Promise to compensate a past voluntary act.
  • Change of Law
  • A new law or government order makes the performance illegal.
  • Example: Export contract becomes void if the government bans exports.
  • Suit for Damages for Non-Acceptance (Section 56)
  • Meaning
  • An action by the seller to claim compensation for loss due to the buyer’s wrongful refusal to accept and
  • pay for the goods.
  • When Available
  • • The buyer refuses to accept and pay for the goods, and
  • • Ownership of the goods has not yet passed to the buyer.
  • Calculation of Damages
  • Usually the difference between the contract price and the market price of the goods at the time of the
  • buyer’s breach.
  • Unconditional Order: Directs a bank to pay a specific sum unconditionally.
  • Crossed Cheque: Cannot be encashed over the counter; must be deposited into an account.
  • • General Crossing: Two parallel lines (may include “& Co.” or “Not Negotiable”).
  • • Special Crossing: Mentions a specific bank between the lines.
  • • Account Payee Crossing: Contains “Account Payee Only”; payable only to the
  • named payee.
  • • Not Negotiable Crossing: Transfer allowed, but transferee gets no better title than
  • transferor.
  • B. Based on Usage or Date
  • Post-Dated Cheque: Dated for a future day; payable only on that date.
  • Unascertained Goods
  • • Definition: Not identified at contract time.
  • • Rule: Passes when goods are unconditionally set aside for the contract with consent.
  • • Examples: Seller sets aside goods, buyer selects from stock, or delivery to carrier without
  • reserving disposal rights.
  • Impact on Organizational Ethics
  • • Reinforcement of Inequality: Bias perpetuates discrimination and hinders career growth for
  • underrepresented groups.
  • • Poor Decision-Making: Distorted performance data leads to wrong choices in promotions
  • training, and resource allocation.
  • • Damaged Culture: Favored treatment fosters distrust, resentment, and reduced collaboration.
  • • Legal and Reputational Risks: Biased appraisals can result in discrimination claims and
  • negative publicity.
  • • Hypocrisy in Leadership: When DE&I ( diversity ,equity and inclusion) values are not reflected
  • in appraisals, employees perceive leadership as insincere.
  • Lack of Transparency: Companies often fail to clearly explain what data is collected, how it
  • is used, and with whom it is shared.
questions.final_answer: Option Types of Contracts

  • 5a. Bais in performance appraisal affect employee morale and organisational ethics.Comment?
  • Bias in performance appraisals occurs when evaluations are influenced by personal preferences
  • stereotypes, or unrelated factors rather than actual performance. It negatively affects both
  • employee morale and organizational ethics.
  • Mitigating Bias in Performance Appraisals
  • • Standardize Evaluation Criteria: Use clear, objective, and specific standards for all employees.
  • • Train Evaluators: Conduct bias-awareness and mitigation training for managers.
  • • Implement Multi-Rater Feedback: Use 360-degree reviews for balanced assessment.
  • • Continuous Feedback and Documentation: Provide regular feedback and maintain performance
  • records throughout the year.
  • • Calibrate Reviews: Managers discuss ratings to ensure fairness across teams.
  • • Promote Self-Assessment: Allow employees to evaluate their own performance to highlight
  • discrepancies.
  • 5b.Explain the ethical concerns related to privacy and data collection in online marketing?
  • Informed Consent Issues
  • Users may agree to complex, lengthy privacy policies without fully understanding them.
  • Many platforms use opt-out tracking instead of explicit opt-in, undermining true consent.
questions.final_answer: Many platforms use opt-out tracking instead of explicit opt-in, undermining true consent

questions.question: Question 4
questions.solution_html:
• Illegal Contract: Forbidden by law; punishable and void.
  • Pledge: Bailment of goods as security for a debt.
  • Lawful: Must not involve illegal, immoral, or prohibited acts.
  • Promissory Estoppel: Enforced if the promisee relied on the promise to their detriment.
  • Impact on Enforceability
  • • Essential Element: Contract without consideration is void (nudum pactum).
  • • Ensures Mutual Obligation: Confirms both parties are bound by promises.
  • • Invalid Consideration: If illegal or illusory, the contract becomes unenforceable.
  • OR
  • 2 2b.Explain discharge of contract by impossibility of performance.
  • bMeaning
  • .T he doctrine allows a contract to be discharged when an unforeseen and uncontrollable event makes
  • performance objectively impossible or meaningless. It is known as the Doctrine of Frustration in
  • common law. The principle is based on “Lex non cogit ad impossibilia” — the law does not compel a
  • person to do the impossible.
  • Grounds for Discharge by Impossibility
  • Non-occurrence of Event
  • If the foundation event of the contract fails to occur.
  • Example: Krell v. Henry (1903) – coronation procession postponed.
  • Payable on Demand: Payment is due immediately upon presentation (unless post-dated).
  • Stale Cheque: Presented after 3 months — no longer valid.
  • Potential Misuse of Data: Collected data can be exploited for manipulation, discrimination
  • or targeted persuasion, harming users.

questions.question: Question 22
questions.solution_html:
• a. Define consideration in contract law. What are the requirements for valid consideration, and
  • ahow does it impact the enforceability of a contract?
  • .C onsideration is a fundamental element of a valid contract, representing the "price of the promise"—
  • the value exchanged between parties. This mutual exchange, also known as quid pro quo, ensures that a
  • contract is a bargained-for transaction rather than a gratuitous promise. Consideration can take many
  • forms, including
  • • A promise: A promise for a future act or forbearance.
  • • An act: The performance of an act.
  • • An abstinence or forbearance: Refraining from doing something one has a legal right to
  • do.
  • Core Requirements

  • the value exchanged between parties. This mutual exchange, also known as quid pro quo, ensures that a
  • contract is a bargained-for transaction rather than a gratuitous promise. Consideration can take many
  • forms, including
  • • A promise: A promise for a future act or forbearance.
  • • An act: The performance of an act.
  • • An abstinence or forbearance: Refraining from doing something one has a legal right to
